name: Rachel and the stolen teraphim
charge: Stealing her father's images, and hiding them under her while she sat upon them
summary: Rachel stole her father's images and hid them beneath the camel's furniture. Laban searched without finding them, while Jacob, unaware of her act, declared that whoever was found with them should not live. No divine sentence for the theft is announced. The household later put away its strange gods before going to Bethel.
offense: She took household gods out of a house she was leaving (Genesis 31:19) and carried them into a covenant family, which is the offense underneath the theft. The concealment compounded it: she placed the images in the camel's furniture, sat upon them, and said she could not rise because the custom of women was upon her (Genesis 31:34-35). The excuse concealed what she had taken; Genesis does not say that she invoked a statute or describe Laban's reasoning about uncleanness. Jacob's ignorance is stated by the record, for Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them (Genesis 31:32), which is why his oath was unwitting.
judgment: No divine sentence for the theft is recorded. Jacob had pronounced that with whomsoever thou findest thy gods (Genesis 31:32), let him not live, without knowing that Rachel was the one who had taken them. She was not found and no judgment is announced. She died bearing Benjamin on the way to Ephrath (Genesis 35:19), but the account does not identify her death as punishment for the theft. Jacob afterwards required the whole household to put away the strange gods that were among them (Genesis 35:2) and buried what the household surrendered under the oak at Shechem (Genesis 35:4). That cleansing addressed the strange gods among them; the passage does not inventory Rachel's stolen images separately.

verses.text: And Laban went to shear his sheep: and Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s.
And now, though thou wouldest needs be gone, because thou sore longedst after thy father’s house, yet wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?
And Jacob answered and said to Laban, Because I was afraid: for I said, Peradventure thou wouldest take by force thy daughters from me.
With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live: before our brethren discern thou what is thine with me, and take it to thee. For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them.
And Laban went into Jacob’s tent, and into Leah’s tent, and into the two maidservants’ tents; but he found them not. Then went he out of Leah’s tent, and entered into Rachel’s tent.
Now Rachel had taken the images, and put them in the camel’s furniture, and sat upon them. And Laban searched all the tent, but found them not.
And she said to her father, Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before thee; for the custom of women is upon me. And he searched, but found not the images.
With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live: before our brethren discern thou what is thine with me, and take it to thee. For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them.

text.text: And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand, and all their earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem.

lawDetails.text: I am the LORD your God, you shall have no other gods besides me.

entries.commentary: Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons, saying, Jacob hath taken away all that was our father's, and of that which was our father's hath he gotten all this glory; and Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and behold, it was not toward him as before. Remember, Laban had just acknowledged, I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake; now he is looking at Jacob sideways because of what his sons said. That is exactly why Jacob said, So shall my righteousness answer for me: he dealt righteously in the open so his dealings would be his answer.
The LORD said unto Jacob, Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred; and I will be with thee. The command to go home came with the promise of the Most High's presence.

Jacob rose up, set his sons and his wives upon camels, and carried away all his cattle and all the goods he had gotten in Padanaram, to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan; he was returning home. Laban went to shear his sheep, and Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's. Remember what we read in Proverbs about beauty: yes, she was fine, but she was a thief. She might have been a fine thief, but she was a thief.

Laban overtook Jacob and asked, Wherefore hast thou stolen my gods? That question tells you what Laban was: Laban was an idolater. The scriptures prove it. Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nachor, and they served other gods. Laban was of the house of Nahor, an idolater just like his fathers. That is why the Most High told Abram to get out from his country and from his kindred: he separated Abram because of what he had set up for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and for us, that we not be idolaters. Jacob answered that he went away because he was afraid Laban would take his daughters from him by force, and said, With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live. For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them.
